title: Ang 152–157: Nanak in Gauri
hookLine: including the night lost in sleep on ang 156
tomorrow: why does a hymn by the fourth Guru end with Nanak's name?

cards: It's 1:52 in the morning. The phone is warm in your hand, the room is dark, and the next video has already started.
Across town, Simran is doing the same thing, and her dad's driving lesson starts at six, in the truck yard, before the rigs roll out. The alarm goes off. She hits snooze.
Then again. When she finally sits up, the yard is quiet and her dad has left for the day. So where did the night go?
Guru Nanak asked that, in Gauri, on Ang 156.

teach.h: A DIAMOND FOR A COWRIE SHELL.
teach.b: His answer, in paraphrase: the night was spent sleeping, the day was spent eating, and a life as precious as a diamond went for a cowrie shell. That's the whole picture in two lines. A diamond, traded for small change.

teach.h: NOT THE SLEEP: WHAT IT SLEPT THROUGH.
teach.b: Notice what the hymn doesn't say. It doesn't say sleep is bad or food is wrong; this is a householder's path, where the langar is a shared meal. The loss isn't the sleeping.
It's sleeping through the one thing the hours were for.

teach.h: YOU NEVER CAME TO KNOW THE NAME.
teach.b: The refrain names it: you never came to know the Name, and later, the hymn warns, comes regret. So who is asleep here? Not just the body.
This hymn treats a life on autopilot as a kind of sleep, and knowing the Name as waking. That's why the early hours matter on this path.
In the Japji, Guru Nanak points to the amrit vela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, as the time for the true Name and its greatness. Not a test you can fail.

teach.h: AMRIT VELA: A DOOR THAT OPENS EARLY.

teach.b: Ang 156 reads like an alarm going off. It isn't angry. It just keeps ringing until you sit up.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks a Sikh to rise in the amrit vela, the early hours, bathe, and remember Waheguru before the morning prayers; Gauri hymns such as the one on Ang 156 are sung as kirtan in the gurdwara.

o: the line where the raga Gauri is named for the first time
a hymn sung only at a Sikh's early morning bath
the page where Guru Nanak's Gauri hymns run on

games.q: the lost night — tap the pairs.

s: Ang 156 says sleeping and eating are wrong
it mourns sleeping through the one thing the hours were for: knowing the Name.
in the Japji, the hours before dawn are the amrit vela
the ambrosial hours, for the true Name and its greatness.
the hymn's refrain warns that regret comes later
you never came to know the Name, and afterward comes regret.

games.q: your friend binge-watched a whole weekend and texts: "that's it, i'm a lost cause." what does Ang 156 actually give her?
o: a wake-up call, not a verdict: the next hour can still go to what matters.
proof the weekend is gone for good, since a shell can't be traded back.
a reason to cut out sleep and fun to make up for lost time.
games.why: the hymn mourns a diamond traded for a shell, but it's written to wake the listener, not to close the door. sleep and food were never the problem.

practice: Sit up the way you would for something that matters: feet on the floor, back tall, eyes soft. With each slow breath out, say Waheguru quietly, the word Sikhs use to remember God.
If that word isn't yours, let the breath be the alarm: in, awake; out, awake.

wordCard.voice: Ang 152: where this stretch of Guru Nanak's Gauri hymns runs on, and on Ang 156, a night lost in sleep.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kauddi, a cowrie shell; on Ang 156, what a diamond-like life is traded for.

carryVoice: Your line: wake up. Not out of guilt; the door just opens early, and it is open now. See you tomorrow.
